Chapter 5: The Road to War—Nationalism, Appeasement, and the Collapse of Peace.
By the middle of the 1930s, something had changed across Europe. The hope and optimism that followed the end of World War One had faded, replaced by a heavy sense of foreboding. Aggressive new regimes were rising in Germany, Italy, and the Soviet Union, casting a long, uncertain shadow over the continent. Old alliances were starting to fall apart, and the organizations designed to keep the peace? They just didn’t seem up to the challenge anymore.
In Germany, a new leadership moved fast to tear down the restrictions of the Treaty of Versailles. Rearmament wasn’t just a policy—it became a national mission. The talk of reviving German pride grew louder and more intense. And for many Germans, worn down by years of humiliation and hardship, this return to a sense of purpose and identity felt like a lifeline. But that renewed energy came at a terrible cost. Persecution of minorities, especially Jews, escalated quickly. Yet, most people turned away, more focused on their own everyday struggles than the suffering of their neighbors.
Meanwhile, in the capitals of Western Europe, leaders faced some agonizing decisions. The memories of the last war were still painfully fresh, and nobody wanted to risk plunging their countries into another nightmare. So, when Germany began annexing its neighbors, the response was hesitant—cautious, even conciliatory. That’s where appeasement came from—a mix of fear and hope, a belief that maybe, just maybe, compromise could steer everyone away from disaster.
For ordinary people, the signs of something terrible building were hard to ignore. Imagine a father worrying about his son being drafted, or a shopkeeper nervously watching the future of his business slip from his hands. Each new headline made the unease grow, yet many clung to the hope that war could still be avoided—that somehow, peace would hold.
Over in the east, the Soviet Union was following its own path—tightening its grip through fear and repression. The purges of the late 1930s sent shockwaves through society. Neighbors vanished overnight, trust disappeared, and what was once the promise of a new society dissolved into an atmosphere of suspicion and terror.
As the 1930s came to an end, everything started moving faster. The annexation of Austria, the breakup of Czechoslovakia, and the shocking Nazi-Soviet Pact made it obvious—the old order in Europe was collapsing. Then, Germany invaded Poland in 1939. That was it—the final step into another devastating war.
The outbreak of conflict was met with a mix of resignation and fear. For so many, it felt like their worst nightmare had come true—a return to horrors everyone thought would never happen again. The lessons of the past just hadn’t been enough to stop catastrophe, and once again, Europe was standing on the edge of destruction.
